passages.t: ‘The earth is the LORD's’, and ‘Who may ascend?’
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “A Psalm of David” (verse 1). Then a great claim: “The earth is the LORD's, and the fullness thereof, the world and all who dwell therein” (verse 1). The reason is that he made it: “For He has founded it upon the seas and established it upon the waters” (verse 2).

Then the question. “Who may ascend the hill of the LORD? Who may stand in His holy place?” (verse 3). And the answer: “He who has clean hands and a pure heart, who does not lift up his soul to an idol or swear deceitfully” (verse 4).

Such a person “will receive blessing from the LORD and vindication from the God of his salvation” (verse 5). “Such is the generation of those who seek Him, who seek Your face, O God of Jacob” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
Jewish memory kept Psalm 24 as a temple song. The Mishnah, an early collection of Jewish teaching, lists the psalm the Levites sang on each day of the week, and Psalm 24 was the song for the first day (Tamid 7:4).

Verses 1 and 2 speak into the beliefs of Israel's neighbours. In the old poems of Ugarit, a Canaanite city on the coast of Syria, the storm god Baal fights the sea god Yam and wins the right to rule. Psalm 24 says simply that the LORD laid the earth on the seas, as a builder lays a foundation. The waters are not his rival. Because he made the world, it all belongs to him, and so does everyone in it.

Verses 3 to 6 are like Psalm 15. Worshippers coming up the hill to the temple ask what God requires, and the answer comes back. ‘Clean hands’ means hands that have done no wrong to others. ‘A pure heart’ means an undivided heart. ‘Lift up his soul to an idol’ means to set your desire on something false, something that is not God.
passages.later:
Paul quotes verse 1 when Christians in Corinth worried about food sold in the market that may have been offered to idols. Eat it, he says, “for, ‘The earth is the Lord's, and the fullness thereof.’” (1 Corinthians 10:26). Everything belongs to God, so nothing is ruined by a false god's name.

Jesus said, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God” (Matthew 5:8), echoing verses 4 and 6.
passages.hard:
Who has clean hands and a pure heart? If the answer is ‘no one’, can anyone go up the hill?

The Old Testament knew this question was hard. That is why God gave sacrifices and a priesthood. Isaiah, seeing God in the temple, cried that he was “a man of unclean lips” and was cleansed by God, not by himself (Isaiah 6:5-7). The note on Psalm 15 says more.

The New Testament gives a fuller answer. Christ “entered heaven itself, now to appear on our behalf in the presence of God” (Hebrews 9:24). He is the one with clean hands and a pure heart, and he brings his people with him. The psalm's standard is not lowered. It is met, and shared.
passages.asks:
Verse 1 asks you to hold what you have loosely. Your home, your money, your time and your body all belong to God first.

Verse 4 asks about your heart's desire. What do you ‘lift up your soul’ to? A false god does not need a statue. It only needs your hope.

passages.t: ‘Lift up your heads, O gates!’ The King of Glory
passages.happening:
Now voices call to the city gates. “Lift up your heads, O gates! Be lifted up, O ancient doors, that the King of Glory may enter!” (verse 7).

Another voice asks, “Who is this King of Glory?” The answer: “The LORD strong and mighty, the LORD mighty in battle” (verse 8).

The call comes again (verse 9), and the question again. This time the answer is fuller: “The LORD of Hosts” is “the King of Glory” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
This part reads like a procession arriving at the city. One group calls for the gates to open. Another, perhaps the gatekeepers, asks who is coming. Many readers connect it with the day David brought the ark of the covenant into Jerusalem “with shouting and the sounding of the ram's horn” (2 Samuel 6:15). Others think it was used again and again at the great feasts. The psalm itself does not say.

City gates were huge, with towers, and the beam across the top could be pictured as a head. The gates are told to lift their heads, to stand taller, as if even they are too small for this King.

‘LORD of Hosts’ means LORD of armies: Israel's armies and the armies of heaven. The title was linked with the ark, the sign of God's presence that went before Israel. The King coming in is not a human king. It is God himself.
passages.later:
In Isaiah's vision the angels cry, “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of Hosts; all the earth is full of His glory” (Isaiah 6:3). John says of Jesus, “We have seen His glory, the glory of the one and only Son from the Father” (John 1:14).

Paul calls Jesus “the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:8). Many Christians read verses 7 to 10 of Jesus going up into heaven after his rising, and picture heaven's gates opening for him.
passages.asks:
The King of Glory comes in. The psalm asks whether your ‘gates’ are open: your home, your plans, your heart. Or are they shut, because a king this big would change things?

You can pray verses 7 to 10 aloud, with others, the way it was first sung: one voice calling, another asking, everyone answering.
